title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
abstract: Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Investigating the Role of Silica Coating toward Artificial Solid Electrolyte Interphase Formation for Na-Ion Anodes
abstract: Sodium-ion batteries (SIB) are a promising cost-effective energy storage solution. However, many anode materials developed for SIB suffer from limited cycle life due to interfacial degradation processes. These lead to the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), a heterogeneous nanolayer resulting from electrolyte decomposition. The SEI is essential for stable long-term cycling; however, its continuous growth progressively decreases performance and may eventually lead to failure of the battery cell. In this work, we examine the effect of an artificial SEI made of thin SiO2 layers on Li4Ti5O12 (LTO) nanoparticles used as a SIB anode. The silica coating results in a 24% improvement in cycling stability after 150 cycles, with minimal effect on rate performance. Detailed characterization by solid-state NMR spectroscopy and electron microscopy shows that the silica layer suppresses the growth and alters the composition of the SEI, reducing the formation of inorganic species, particularly NaF and NaF-rich components. Using dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP)-enhanced NMR, a technique that greatly boosts NMR sensitivity, we show how the coating alters the SEI structure, from a layered inorganic core with an organic shell on uncoated LTO to a mixed mosaic-like SEI. Furthermore, we find SEI formation beneath the SiO2 layer, providing molecular-level insights into the interfacial processes. This study provides routes for the design of improved SEI layers, paving the way for the development of more durable and high-performance SIB cells for future energy storage applications.

title: Biochemical reassessment of the activation of PANK1 by SGLT2 inhibitors
abstract: Although SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) show cardiovascular benefits in addition to glycemic control, their molecular target for cardiovascular effect remains unclear. A recent study reported that two SGLT2i, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, directly activate pantothenate kinase 1 (PANK1), which mediate their cardioprotective effect. PANK1 phosphorylates pantothenate with ATP to yield 4'-phosphopantothenate and ADP, representing the rate-limiting enzyme of coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis. We therefore reassessed this claim using purified recombinant human PANK1. The malachite green assay detected free inorganic phosphate (Pi) but neither ADP nor 4'-phosphopantothenate and its signals do not reflect PANK1 activity. In the ADP-Glo assay, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin did not stimulate PANK1 under either basal conditions or acetyl-CoA feedback inhibition, while the activator PZ-2891 enhanced the activity of PANK1. These results show that SGLT2i do not directly activate PANK1, challenging the proposed PANK1-dependent cardioprotection mechanism.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of the Proposed 1,4-Dihydropyridinate Intermediate with a Nickel-Pincer Nucleotide Cofactor Model Complex
abstract: The nickel pincer nucleotide (NPN) cofactor was structurally characterized in lactate racemase in 2014, and it is now known that NPN is important in a superfamily of enzymes responsible for isomerization of α-hydroxyacids and also important in other hydride transfer reactions across bacteria and archaea. A decade of biochemical and theoretical studies have led to proposals for the mechanism of reaction for the NPN, but structural or spectroscopic characterization of a well-defined intermediate in the mechanisms has been elusive.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A molecular glue degrader-antibody conjugate for HER2-targeted cyclin K degradation
abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase 12 (CDK12) is an attractive therapeutic target due to its critical role in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage response and is frequently co-amplified with ERBB2 (HER2) in breast cancer. CDK12 forms an active complex with its obligate partner cyclin K (CCNK), and pharmacological degradation of CCNK has emerged as a promising strategy for disrupting CDK12-dependent transcriptional programs. However, the broad expression and essential functions of the CDK12/CCNK complex may limit the therapeutic window of highly potent molecular glue degraders. Here, we investigate whether antibody-mediated delivery can impart cellular selectivity to a molecular glue degrader through targeting the HER2 receptor. Molecular glues lack the modular architecture of PROTACs, thus linker placement can be the central design problem. We designed SAS1001, a CCNK molecular glue degrader with a solvent-exposed piperazine primed for linker attachment. SAS1001 induced potent and ubiquitin-proteasome system-dependent degradation of CCNK and inhibited proliferation in a range of breast cancer cells. Conjugation to trastuzumab (Tz) generated the HER2-targeted degrader-antibody conjugate Tz-SS2009, which internalized preferentially in HER2-positive cells and produced enhanced CCNK degradation and antiproliferative effects, relative both to HER2-negative cells and to an isotype-matched non-targeting conjugate. Whole proteome analysis further demonstrated CCNK depletion and revealed downstream changes consistent with established roles of the CDK12/CCNK complex in transcriptional regulation. These findings demonstrate that antibody-mediated delivery can redistribute the cellular activity of a potent molecular glue degrader towards antigen-positive cells. In the CR8/DS18 purine series, substitution at a solvent-exposed position preserved CCNK degradation when the degrader was delivered on a full-length IgG. More broadly, this work extends antibody-directed degradation beyond the CRBN-based glues that have dominated the field and illustrates how structural characterization of a glue scaffold can identify a linker attachment point that does not compromise activity.

title: Tuning the Molecular Electronic Structure of Polysaccharides: A Comparative DFT Study of Chemically Modified Chitosan and Cellulose Derivatives
abstract: The rational molecular design of functionalized polysaccharides for advanced electronic and sensing applications necessitates a comprehensive mapping of their electronic chemical space. In this study, we report a high-throughput computational screening of 115 chemically modified chitosan and cellulose derivatives. Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) energies, HOMO–LUMO energy gaps (ΔE gap ), and a comprehensive suite of global conceptual density functional theory (DFT) descriptors were computed for isolated oligomeric models at the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) level with SMD implicit solvation.

title: Operando pH Measurements of OER within a Porous Oxygen-Evolving Electrode
abstract: Three-dimensional porous electrodes, such as those in membrane electrode assemblies, are widely employed in electrochemical devices due to their high surface area and achievable current density. The heterogeneous internal structure of the porous electrode microenvironment engenders local concentration gradients owing to mass transport constraints. Localized microenvironments with properties distinct from those of the bulk solution are especially prevalent for electrocatalytic reactions that produce or consume protons, as local basic or acidic environments may significantly influence the energy efficiency and selectivity of proton-coupled electron transfer reactions that are necessary for small-molecule activation. Here, we develop an operando method employing polymer-bound fluorescent sensors (PFS) to directly quantify local pH and the internal proton gradient in a porous electrode for the oxygen evolution reaction catalyzed by IrOx supported on indium-tin oxide (ITO). The PFS uncovers notable pH gradients within a 3-μm-thick layer of the OER electrode in unbuffered electrolyte, even at low current density. Proton transport dynamics were found to be influenced significantly by the proton adsorption properties of the ITO support, revealing a previously unrecognized role of the oxide support in modifying the local pH gradient. The PFS method should prove useful in the study and evaluation of electrochemical devices, including fuel cells, bipolar and other ion-conducting membranes, and electrolyzers.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ion-Association Design Decouples Linearity and Dynamic Range in Organic Electrochemical Synapses
abstract: Organic electrochemical synaptic transistors (OESTs) are promising neuromorphic devices, but simultaneously achieving highly linear analog weight updates and a wide dynamic range remains fundamentally limited by a severe trade-off in uncontrolled interface doping kinetics. Although multicomponent electrolytes offer a pathway to tune ion behavior, a predictive framework capable of overcoming this strict trade-off remains unexplored due to the highly nonlinear nature of interionic interactions.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Experimental and computational mapping reveals preferential nanobody targeting of the intracellular cavity of the amino acid transporter BasC
abstract: Nanobodies are valuable tools for stabilizing and investigating membrane transporters, but the systematic characterization of large nanobody collections remains experimentally demanding. Here, we combined biochemical and transport assays, experimental structural data and AlphaFold3 modelling to characterize a repertoire of 29 nanobodies targeting the bacterial amino acid transporter BasC. By exploiting the random orientation and asymmetric apparent substrate affinities of BasC in proteoliposomes, comparison of nanobody-mediated influx and efflux inhibition enabled experimental assignment of binding sidedness. The collection showed a marked bias towards inhibition from the intracellular face, whereas only two, Nb58 and Nb78, were identified as extracellular binders. Compatibility assays and a 6.1 [A] crystallographic map of the BasC-Nb53-Nb58 complex supported the simultaneous binding of Nb53 and Nb58 to opposite sides of the transporter and validated the functional sidedness assignment. AlphaFold3 generated high-confidence interaction models for 16 of the 29 complexes. Ten of these models targeted the large intracellular cavity, revealing recurrent epitope clusters. The predicted binding modes of Nb53, Nb71 and Nb74 agreed with available experimental structures, supporting the accuracy of these predictions. Notably, these three nanobodies had previously provided the most informative structural and smFRET data. Our results show that transport-based sidedness measurements together with confidence-filtered structural predictions can define the functional and structural landscape of a nanobody repertoire. This integrated approach may provide a virtual structural screening strategy to prioritize nanobodies, identify dominant epitope regions and select potentially compatible combinations for experimental and structural studies.

title: High Temperature Acetylene-to-Ethylene Hydrogenation over Pd: A Combined Experimental, Machine Learning Potential, and DFT Investigation
abstract: Selective hydrogenation of acetylene to ethylene at temperatures relevant to direct non-oxidative methane conversion (DNMC) could enable downstream upgrading without intermediate cooling and reheating. Here, we combine experimental catalyst screening, machine learning potential (MLP) simulations, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to identify Pd surface motifs responsible for acetylene hydrogenation at 850°C.

title: Synergistic Construction of Axial and Central Chirality via an Organocatalytic Three-Component Reaction Involving In Situ-Formed α-Functionalized Alcohols
abstract: The synergistic construction of both axial and central chirality represents a formidable challenge in asymmetric catalysis. Herein, we report an organocatalytic three-component reaction among N-aryl-2-substituted anilines, 2-oxo-2-arylacetaldehydes, and indoles, which enables the de novo synthesis of axially and centrally chiral N-(2-substituted phenyl)benzo[e]indol-1-ones. This transformation features the in situ formation of α-functionalized alcohols, followed by a 1,2-addition of the resulting iminium species.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Iron-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Phosphonylation of Aliphatic Carboxylic Acids with Succinimidyl Phosphites as Bifunctional Reagents
abstract: Aliphatic carboxylic acids are abundant, stable, and cost-effective, rendering them ideal substrates for site-specific C(sp3)–P bond formation via decarboxylative pathways. However, the direct catalytic decarboxylative phosphonylation of these acids remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report that the use of dialkyl succinimidyl phosphites as bifunctional reagents enables the iron-catalyzed decarboxylative phosphonylation of aliphatic carboxylic acids to proceed smoothly at room temperature under visible light irradiation.

title: Redox-Responsive 2′-OH Acylation for Late-Stage RNA Conjugation
abstract: Covalent RNA conjugates have proved effective in basic research and therapy, yet their broader use is limited by synthetic complexity and high costs. Here, we describe a modular, redox-responsive strategy for late-stage conjugation of diverse biofunctional ligands onto RNA. We show that acylation of RNA 2′-OH groups with disulfide-containing acyl moieties enables thiol–disulfide exchange with thiol-bearing ligands, including N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), peptides, biotin, and captopril.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society
